title: How do you answer "What is your biggest weakness?" honestly and well?
description: How to answer the weakness question in consulting interviews, with weak and strong example answers and how to show self-awareness.
hook: You answer "What is your biggest weakness?" by naming a real weakness that would not stop you doing the job, giving one example of when it hurt your work, and spending most of the answer on the specific habit you now use to manage it and the evidence it is working. The question is less about the weakness than about self-awareness. Interviewers want someone who knows where they struggle and is actively doing something about it.
body:
What the interviewer is testing

Consulting runs on feedback. You get it often, and the people who do well are the ones who hear criticism and change. The weakness question is a preview of that. The interviewer is asking: can you see your own patterns, are you honest about them, and do you have a system for improving?

How to choose your weakness

  • Real. Something colleagues or managers have actually told you, or that you have noticed repeatedly.
  • Relevant but not fatal. It should matter at work, but not undermine the core of the job. "I struggle with numbers" is a risky choice for a consulting interview; "I used to avoid giving direct feedback" is not.
  • Managed. You should have a habit you use to keep it in check, and an example of using it.

A weak answer

I'm a perfectionist, so I sometimes spend too long making my work perfect.

Why it falls short: it is probably the most common answer of all. It sounds rehearsed, dodges a real weakness and has no example or fix.

A strong answer

This example is illustrative; use your own.

I used to avoid giving direct feedback to colleagues, because I worried about upsetting them. On one project that meant a teammate kept making the same error in our analysis until it reached the client. Since then I've made it a habit to give feedback within a day, starting with what went well and then one specific thing to change. At my last review I asked my manager whether she'd noticed a difference, and she said it had clearly improved, though it still takes effort for me.

Why it works: a real weakness that matters at work, a concrete consequence, a specific habit, honest evidence of progress, and an admission that it is not completely solved, which makes the whole answer more believable.

A second example

Earlier in my career I waited too long before showing early work to my manager, because I wanted every figure reconciled first. On one project we only discovered a mismatch in how the client defined "active customers" after I'd spent two days rebuilding a model. Now, at the start of any piece of work, I share the question, the definitions and a rough first calculation, and agree the key assumptions before refining. I still care about accuracy, but I no longer treat a polished model as the first useful thing I deliver.

This one works because the habit is observable: early assumption checks and rough-cut reviews. An interviewer can ask when you last used it and what happened, and you should have an answer ready. It is also a weakness that matters in consulting, where teams share rough work early and often.

The shape to follow

  1. Name it in one sentence, as a behaviour, not a personality trait.
  2. One example of when it caused a problem.
  3. The habit you now use to manage it. This is the longest part.
  4. Evidence that it is working, such as feedback or a later situation that went better.
  5. Honesty that you are still working on it.

Aim for 45 to 60 seconds. Longer, and it starts to sound like a confession.

Common mistakes

  • The humble brag. "I care too much", "I work too hard". Interviewers have heard them countless times.
  • A weakness with no fix. Naming a flaw and stopping there leaves the interviewer with only the flaw.
  • A fatal weakness. Avoid anything that goes to the core of the job, such as dislike of ambiguity or of working in teams.
  • Claiming it is fully solved. If it has vanished, it is no longer your weakness, and the answer sounds too neat.
  • Choosing what you think they want. Pick something you have genuinely worked on, so you can handle follow-ups.

Try it now

1. Rewrite this as a behaviour: "My weakness is that I'm impatient."

Show the answer

"I tend to push for a decision before everyone has had their say. In one project meeting that meant a quieter colleague's concern only came out after we'd committed. Now I ask each person for their view before I suggest a way forward."

2. Is "I'm not comfortable with ambiguity" a good choice for a consulting interview?

Show the answer

Risky. Ambiguous problems are the core of the job, so it can make the interviewer doubt your fit. Choose a weakness that matters but sits around the edges of the role, such as delegation or giving feedback.

3. Write your answer in the five-part shape and time it.

Show the answer

Check that the habit is the longest part and that it is something an observer could see you do. Check that your evidence is specific: a named piece of feedback or a later situation. Keep it under 60 seconds.

Where to practise next

Use a different story for the failure question, which interviewers often ask in the same conversation. Add both to your story bank with the fit interview guide, check the most common fit questions, and prepare questions to ask at the end.
